Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 1:

(p-195) Surat al-Waqi'ah (The Inevitable Event)

Its purpose is to explain the states of the three categories mentioned in al-Rahman: for the allies (awliya'), from among the foremost (al-sabiqun) and the latter (al-lahiqun), and for the enemies who oppose (al-mushaqqin), from among the open opponents (al-musarihin) and the hypocrites (al-munafiqun), from both the two weighty things (al-thaqalan: humankind and jinn). This is to show the complete power in action, by choice, which the ending of al-Rahman indicated through affirming perfection; and the ending of this surah indicates it through exalting God (al-tanzih) by negating everything that involves deficiency, and then affirming Him with the attribute of greatness together with all perfection, both in beauty (al-jamal) and majesty (al-jalal). Had people been equal, that would not have belonged to the sublime wisdom, for their equality would become a doubt for the people of nature (ahl al-tabi'ah). Its name, al-Waqi'ah, indicates this through reflection upon its verses; and what the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) relates to it is: (In the name of God), to whom belongs all perfection, so that people differ in their states; (the All-Merciful), who encompassed all with the blessing of eloquence and distinguished between those who accept it among the people of turning away and the people of turning toward; (the Most Merciful), who brought the people of His party near to the people of His nearness, so they triumphed through the excellences of speech and deeds.

* *

When He (glory be to Him) classified people in that [surah] into three categories — criminals, foremost, and latter — and concluded with the reason for that, namely that He is the One of retribution and generosity, He explained their states in this surah and clarified the time in which His generosity and His retribution would appear with the utmost clarity, as mentioned in al-Rahman. So He said, building upon what the context guided to — that its implied meaning is: all of that will occur as an occurrence whose knowledge is shared by the elite and the common: **"When the Inevitable Event occurs"** (idha waqa'at al-waqi'ah), meaning the event that must occur, and no other event deserves to be called "the Event" (al-waqi'ah) by the particle of definiteness (lam al-kamal) and the intensive ta' (ta' al-mubalaghah). It is the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah), from which will come the Great Resurrection (al-ba'th al-akbar), which is the Resurrection gathering all creation for judgment among them in the manifest singularity, for which no claimant to partnership exists in any way whatsoever. It is also permissible that "idha" be governed by an elided verb, so that the soul may go in every direction with it, and it would then be more terrifying, meaning: when it occurs, there will be matters that the bounds of enumeration cannot contain.

When this was the case, its meaning being the Hour concerning which the decree has been finalized that it must come to pass, he expressed it by beginning with an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), saying: ﴿There is no denying (lit. no lying) about its occurrence﴾, that is, the realization of its existence. ﴿Kadhibah﴾ [i.e., a lie / denial] here is a verbal noun (masdar) expressed by the form of the active participle for emphasis (mubalaghah), meaning that there is nothing in its circumstances to which a lie could be attributed, no falsehood walks in it at all, and it is not tolerated; rather, whatever it has announced will come has come without anything turning it back, and whatever it has announced as negated has been negated, so nothing brings it about. He established its greatness and affirmed the raising of affairs within it with his saying, reporting about an omitted subject:

﴿Khafidah﴾ (abasing): it abases whomever Allah wills to abase, from among the great ones of the people of the Fire and others, and from among what He wills of mountains and other things, down to the lowest of the low. ﴿Rafi'ah﴾ (exalting): it exalts the weak among the people of Paradise and others from their dwellings and other things that He wills, up to ʿIlliyyin, none can repel His command or reverse His judgment.

Since in this there is such terror as would pierce the attentive hearts, He reinforced it with His saying, and added, also, what He wills of it, with His saying, substituting for the first temporal clause some of what enters into lowering and raising: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾. That is, all of it, despite its vastness and heaviness, with the utmost ease. ﴿Shaken (rajjan)﴾, that is, it was quaked with a severe quaking, with violence, so that it sank and rose, then it was convulsed along with its inhabitants with a severe convulsion. Al-Baghawi said: "Rajj" in the language means "tahrik" (agitation, shaking).

When he had mentioned its disturbing motion, he followed it with its ultimate end, saying: ﴿And the mountains will be pulverized﴾, meaning they will be crumbled, despite their hardness and immensity, at the slightest sign; their stone will be mixed with their dust until they become one thing; they will become like carded wool, and they will be set in motion, passing by as clouds pass, ﴿pulverized﴾.

"So it became" — that is, because of that — ﴿dust scattered﴾, meaning dust in the utmost state of dissolution. To its extreme fineness he alluded by the form of the passive, saying ﴿scattered﴾ — that is, dispersed and separated of itself, without any need for air to disperse it. It is like what is seen in a sunbeam when it enters through a window opening.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 7:

When he had mentioned the ultimate end of its frightening and terrifying beginnings, he mentioned the beginnings of its ultimate ends, saying: ﴿And you shall be﴾, that is, you shall be divided according to what was in your natures and dispositions in the world, ﴿into three groups﴾, that is, kinds, none of which is complete in its wisdom except by being [two divisions]: a higher one and one below it, so that this would be more indicative of the perfection of power. They are the People of the Right Hand, who are divided into the foremost (sabiqun), who are the muqarrabun (those brought near), and into those who follow, who are the righteous (al-abrar), or the People of the Right (ashab al-yamin). It seems that they are of the "people of the middle" (ulu al-qalb alladhi huwa al-adl al-sawa), from the People of the Left to the end of the People of the Right. So the People of the Equal (ashab al-sawa') are the muqarrabun, and the rest of the People of the Right are the People of the Right (ashab al-yamin), and the People of the Left (ashab al-mash'ama) are the People of the Third Group. Each of the three is divided into a higher and a lower part, and the three divisions have been made clear at the end of the surah. Al-Baydawi said: Every kind, when it occurs or is mentioned together with another kind, is a pair (zawj).

When he had divided them into three categories and elaborated on their division, he described their conditions. He began this by informing them that the (true) report is not like the (mere) report, just as the (direct) sight is not like the (mere) trace. So He said: ﴿Then the companions of the right hand﴾, meaning the direction of the right, its place, and its deeds. Then he magnified their matter by expressing wonder at their condition, with His words, alerting (the reader) that they are [worthy] of being asked about, given what the right hand conveys of goodness and blessing. How much more so when He expresses it with an intensive form, so He said: ﴿What﴾, which is the second subject (mubtada' thani), ﴿are the companions of the right hand?﴾, meaning the direction of the right, its place, and its deeds. The sentence is a predicate (khabar) concerning the first (subject), and the linking element is the repetition of the subject by its own wording. Abu Hayyan, may God Most High have mercy on him, said: "This is most often found in contexts of awe and glorification."

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: Since the warning was given in the two preceding surahs, and the affirmation was made through the great proofs, and at the end of Surat al-Qamar He informed (us) that everything that occurs in the world happens by His decree and His predestination, ﴿Indeed, We have created everything with measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49] (p-199) ﴿And everything they have done is in the scriptures﴾ [al-Qamar: 52]. And He, glorified is He, informed them in al-Waqi'ah of their division in the Hereafter, so He opened the mention of the Hour with ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1], up to His words: ﴿And you were three kinds of pairs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 7]. Thus this surah is devoted to defining their conditions in the Hereafter, and it is introduced with that, just as in this surah He had earlier defined their condition in this abode. What came up in the three surahs, proceeding in a manner other than this style, is by way of the requirement of calling to desire and fear, as a kindness to the servants and as mercy, and their openings are founded upon what I have mentioned, explicitly and not allusively, and comprehensively and not by indication and hint. For this reason, God Most High said at the end of the Hereafter narratives in this surah: ﴿This is their welcome on the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 56], thereby informing that this is their condition on the Day of Recompense, and He had already presented their worldly condition in the two preceding surahs, and (this surah) affirms the earlier definition afterward. That is His words: ﴿As for if he was of those brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88], to its end. Ended.

When He had mentioned those who are saved, in both their categories, He followed them with their opposites, saying: ﴿And the companions of the left hand﴾, that is, the direction of misfortune, its place, and its deeds. Then He magnified their sin, saying: ﴿What are the companions of the left hand?﴾, that is, because they are deserving of being asked about what befell them of misfortune, evil, and ruin, by His great power, which drove them to the recompense they reached, which no sensible person would bring upon himself, nor even a beast, despite the sound intellects and great reasoning with which they were endowed; and He preserved the foremost ones from forsaking the way of these, so He brought them to everlasting bliss.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 10:

When he had mentioned the two categories, and each of them had two divisions, he mentioned the foremost of the people of the first category, as an encouragement toward their best condition, and did not divide the people of the left hand (al-mash'amah), as a warning against the evil of their final state. So he said: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾; that is, in the works of obedience, are those who are the owners of the two first gardens in (the Mercy of) the Most Merciful, and they are the people of nearness (ahl al-qalb). ﴿The foremost﴾; that is, they are the ones who deserve the description of being foremost, and not others, because it is a rank higher than their rank, and therefore they outpaced to their rank, which is their garden. They are of two kinds, as will come from al-Razi. And from al-Mahdawi that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The foremost are those who, when they are given the truth, accept it, and when they are asked for it, they give it, and they judge for the people as they judge for themselves."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 11:

When he had explained the lofty status of these people and attributed the precedence to them, he expressed it by setting them apart from the others with his words: ﴿Those are the ones brought near﴾. That is, those of very high rank from among those who are the companions of the right hand (al-maymanah). ﴿The ones brought near (al-muqarrabun)﴾: that is, those whom Allah the Exalted chose for precedence, so He brought them near by His nearness, or He bestowed favour upon them [by His nearness]. Had it not been for His action in bringing them near, they would not have been foremost.

Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': The muqarrabun have been freed from their selves, so all their actions are for Allah, in religion and in worldly affairs, concerning the right of Allah and the right of people, and both of these are, in their view, the right of Allah. The world, for them, is their hereafter, because they watch what appears to them of His malakut (dominion), and so they receive it with contentment and submission. They are of two kinds. One kind has hearts bewildered in His majesty and greatness, whose awe has taken possession of them, so the Truth employs them. Another kind has loosened the reins of their hearts, so the matter is easier for them, because [they have] come to be near, in their hearts, to this lowliness, and their station is higher, so he is the trustee of Allah on His earth. Thus the matter is easier for him, because he has surpassed (this) — end of quote.

Then he explained their nearness to Him by His saying: ﴿In gardens of bliss﴾, meaning: the bliss to which there is no bliss beyond, for there is no turbidity in it in any way, nor anything that spoils it. The other category among them are the ones who are far off and who oppose (the truth), from the companions of the left hand (al-mashʾamah); those are the ones upon whom is anger, the far-removed. Beneath them are the astray, the distant, and they are the companions of the left (ash-shimal).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 13:

When he mentioned the foremost (al-sabiqun), he detailed them, saying: ﴿A multitude﴾, i.e., a large, good group, and al-Baghawi said: al-thullah (multitude) is a group whose number is not limited,

﴿from among the former peoples﴾, and they are the prophets who passed before, upon them be prayer and peace, and those who believed in them without an intermediary, may Allah be pleased with them.

﴿And a few from the later generations.﴾ These are those who believed in Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) without an intermediary, may Allah be pleased with them. The prophets, peace be upon them, numbered one hundred and twenty thousand and more. When Moses (peace be upon him) left Egypt, those who believed in him among the fighting men, those aged above twenty and below eighty, numbered six hundred thousand. So what do you suppose about those beyond them, the elders, those under twenty among the followers, the children, and the women? How much more so about the rest of the prophets, peace be upon them, the renewers among the Children of Israel and others.

It has been said: "The thullah (large group) and the qalil (small group) are both from this ummah." This was narrated by al-Tabarani and Ibn 'Adi from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. In its chain is Aban ibn Abi 'Ayyash, who is matruk (abandoned, rejected by the hadith critics). It was also narrated by Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Musaddad ibn Musarhad, Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Ibrahim al-Harbi, and al-Tabarani, through the narration of 'Ali ibn Zayd (p-٢٠٢), who is weak, from 'Uqba ibn Suhban, from Abu Bakra, may Allah be pleased with him, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) and as a mawquf (ending with a Companion). The mawquf version is more correct. Applying it to this ummah, whether it is marfu' or mawquf, is sound and beyond dispute. Thus all the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, are from this thullah, and likewise those who followed them in goodness up to the end of the third century. None can count them except Allah, the Exalted.

It is well known that the matter diminished after that, until the foremost ones among people became fewer than the few, as Islam returned to the state in which it began, that of strangeness: "Islam began as a stranger and will return to being a stranger, so blessed are the strangers."

It is also permissible to read it as follows: and a thullah (a large multitude, destroyed) from the earlier generations, namely the obstinate ones of the past nations; and a few from the later generations, namely the obstinate ones of this ummah.

When he had mentioned the foremost in good (with their two categories), alluding to the foremost in evil (with their two categories), he mentioned the reward of the people of good, so that the reward of those others might be known from it. So he said, clarifying that they are kings, but their kingship is not an object of rivalry or envy; rather all of it is met with affection and purity: ﴿on thrones﴾, which are the high seats made for comfort and honour that pleasure a person, and which are the sign of kingship, namely the throne; ﴿woven [with gold]﴾, that is, woven in a double weave, set one within another, closely woven, admirable like a coat of mail, but their weaving is with gold, detailed with jewels of pearls and rubies.

"When He mentioned the couches and explained their greatness, He mentioned their purpose, saying: ﴿reclining upon them﴾ (p-203) — that is, reclining in the posture of one sitting cross-legged, or other than that, or reclining on the side, or other than that — ﴿upon them﴾. And since a gathering, when it is large, involves some of its people turning their backs to one another, He informed that the assemblies of the people of Paradise are otherwise, saying: ﴿facing one another﴾. So there is no distance and no turning away: none of them looks at the back of another, and none of them dislikes another."

Since reclining can make standing difficult for the one who reclines, He said: ﴿They will be attended by immortal youths﴾, meaning, for the purpose of providing everything they need, ﴿youths﴾ of the finest form, dress, and appearance, ﴿immortal﴾, whom God has decreed to remain in the state they are in. Al-Baghawi said: The Arabs say of someone who has grown old, and of someone whose hair has turned grey, "He is mukhalladun (made eternal)." He said: al-Hasan said: They are the children of the people of this world, who had no good deeds for which they would be rewarded, nor evil deeds for which they would be punished, because there is no childbearing in Paradise; so they are the servants of the people of Paradise.

Since this praise was extremely eloquent yet concise, and since it contained, alongside the conveying of what they receive, a stirring toward the like of their deeds, and since eating, which is among the greatest of needs, was indicated by the great praise—of which resting on couches is part, for it is known that it is the custom of kings not to mount them except after satisfying their need from it—nothing remained after it except what need calls for of drinks and what follows them. God the Exalted said: ﴿with cups﴾, that is, goblets with round mouths, without handles or spouts, so that no obstacle prevents the drinker from drinking from them from whatever direction he wishes, and he does not need to turn the vessel to the position from which he took it in order to drink. It is possible that the beginning with drink (p-204) is because of the hardships they endured from thirst, as with one who drinks from a pool; in that case it would be before eating, and God knows best. ﴿and ewers﴾, that is, vessels that have handles and spouts, containing kinds of drinks that the souls desire and that delight the eyes. ﴿and a cup﴾, that is, a vessel prepared for drinking, and the drink itself within it.

Since the drink is general, He specified it by His saying: ﴿from a flowing spring﴾, that is, wine that flows, pure with the purity of water, whose pressing is not burdened upon anyone, but rather it gushes forth as water gushes.

When he had established its benefit and what makes one long for it, he negated what repels from it, and said: ﴿They will not be affected with any splitting [of the head]﴾, meaning a splitting that would require turning away from it, namely a headache, nor any dispersal out of weariness. ﴿Nor will they be intoxicated﴾, meaning their minds will not be taken away in any way, that is, their drink will not knock them down. It is from *nazafat al-bi'r* (the well was drained), when all of its water has been drained out, and *nazafa fulan* (so-and-so), meaning his mind went or he became drunk. The two verbs, *yuṣaddaʿūna* (يُصَدَّعُونَ) and *yunzafūna* (يُنْـزِفُونَ), are in the passive voice, because there is no need to know the agent. Al-Razi said in *al-Lawami'*: al-Sadiq said: "Their minds are not distracted from the sources of the realities upon them, and they are never absent from the assemblies of contemplation in any state."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 20:

When he began with the most delicious of what aids digestion for eating, he followed it with what comes next in that category, which digestion calls for, stating it explicitly after alluding to it, so he said: ﴿And fruit of what they choose﴾. That is, it is among them in such a way that, if there were among them both good and other kinds, and they chose and took great care in selecting, it would be of what is subject to such choosing.

When he had mentioned what custom has established as eaten purely for pleasure, he followed it with what custom holds is for sustenance, though there too it is also for pleasure alone, so he said: (p-205) ﴿and the flesh of birds﴾. Since among bird flesh there is something that is shunned, he guarded against that by his words ﴿of what they desire﴾, meaning, of the utmost desire, such that they find at its end the same pleasure they find at its beginning.

Since nothing is more appealing after eating and drinking than intercourse, He said, conjoining [this clause] to ﴿young boys﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17]: ﴿and wide-eyed maidens﴾, meaning: they will circulate among them. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive, conjoining it to ﴿couches﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 15], since women carry the sense of reclining, for they are called "bedding" (firash).

Since "mithl" (likeness) originally means the very thing itself, as has passed in the commentary on Surah al-Shura, He said: ﴿like pearls well-guarded﴾, that is, like the persons of pearls kept hidden, meaning preserved within the shell from whatever might soil it.

Once he had gone to the full extent in describing their reward with goodness and purity, this indicated that their deeds were likewise, because the recompense is of the same kind as the deed. So the Exalted said: ﴿A reward﴾, meaning that this was done for them as a recompense ﴿for what they used to do﴾ by disposition and nature ﴿working﴾, meaning they continually renewed their work in the manner of constancy.

When He established perfection for it (Paradise) and assigned it to them, He negated imperfection from it, saying: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk﴾, meaning in any state whatsoever, ﴿nor any sinful speech﴾, meaning anything that is of no benefit, for indeed the most crushing... with that (being) the All-Hearing, the All-Wise. That is it. And al-laghw (idle talk) is that which falls away (is worthless). ﴿Nor any sinful speech﴾, meaning anything through which sin is incurred, or any attribution to sin. Rather, all their movements and stillnesses are [all] the pleasure of God. Nothing has cut off the hearts of the wayfarers to God except these two traits: at times one of them builds what benefits him, striving in the building, when his nature overcomes him so that he demolishes most of what he built; and while he thinks he has drawn near, when he realizes by the like of that that he has gone far, his abode has become distant and his place of visitation remote. So God is the One sought for help.

When the exception served as the criterion of generality, He brought His saying in the form of an exception: ﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾. That is, it (the saying) is in the utmost gentleness and tenderness, through what is indicated by the derived form built upon what precedes it of excellences, together with what the root qawala (q-w-l) indicates. When the listener yearned for it through the expression mentioned, He explained it by His saying: ﴿Peace﴾, and He indicated its permanence by repeating it, saying: ﴿Peace﴾. That is: no saying arises in the soul or appears to the senses from them except one indicating safety, because there is no ruin in it at all. He placed it in the manner of the connected exception (istithna' muttasil, connected exception), indicating that if there is any idle talk in it, it is only that, which reassures them, delights them and gives them good news, and at the same time it indicates the goodness of companionship, the beauty of fellowship, the refinement of character and the purity of affection.

When Glorified is He had completed the first division, the heart-centred and mid-ranking group among the three (those who are foremost, the companions of the right, and the companions of the left, with its two sub-divisions), and had mentioned in their reward what belongs to the people of the cities, which they cannot reach, He followed it with the second group, which is lower than them in that respect, and which is, and God knows best, the righteous (al-abrar). They too are of two kinds. He mentioned in their reward something of the same kind as what belongs to the people of the desert, the furthest of what they can imagine and desire. So He said: ﴿And the companions of the right﴾. Then He magnified their matter and raised their praise to glorify their reward, and to point out that they are worthy of being asked about their condition, for they are in the utmost state of admiration. So He said: ﴿What are the companions of the right!﴾

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 28:

When he expressed about them with what made clear that they are people of strength and diligence in deeds, and of blessing in the gathering of their conditions, he mentioned their living, beginning with fruit, because the entire living of Paradise is enjoyment of fruits (tafakkuh), mentioning from it what grows in the lands of the Arabs without effort, with no planting or service. He indicated the abundance of what he mentions by making it their container (zarf), saying, without mentioning the couch of kingship upon which He bestowed favour on those brought near to the King, and he did not add to that food and what accompanies it anything that might be imagined for beasts: ﴿Among lote-trees﴾, meaning trees of jujube (nabq) whose branches hang down from the intensity of their bearing, from "sadara al-sha'r" (he let his hair hang down) ﴿without thorns﴾, meaning that it has no thorns and no pits, such that its branches bend from the intensity of the load, from "khadada al-shawk" (he cut off the thorn), and "al-ghusn" (he bent the branch) while it is fresh. In the mention of this there is an alert that everything in Paradise that has no benefit in it, or in which there is some kind of harm, has no existence there, because Paradise was created only for delight.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 29:

When he had mentioned what grows in the mountains, in the places without water and in the sands, he followed it with what grows only over water, as a sign that their dwellings are in the utmost ease and abundance of water. So He said: ﴿And talh (acacia trees)﴾, that is, banana trees or palm trees. Al-Hasan said: a tree that has cool shade and pleasant fragrance. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda said: large trees that have thorns. It was also said: it is Umm Ghaylan, which has abundant blossom. It is related from Abu Turab al-Nakhshabi that he was travelling with a group of Sufis upon the path of complete reliance upon God (tawakkul), and they went hungry for days. He said: "Do you want to eat?" They said: "Yes." So he struck his hand upon an Umm Ghaylan tree, and behold, there were clusters of bananas upon it. They ate, except for one young man among them, who said: "I will not eat, nor will I accompany you after this, because I used to travel without a known provision, and now you have become my known provision; whenever I am hungry, my soul turns to you."

﴿Mandud (layered, arranged)﴾, that is, arranged with fruit from its top to its bottom, piled one upon another in an order that is most admirable. In the Qamus (the lexicon) it is said: "Talh: a great tree. Talh (also tal') and banana: the spathe of the palm is a thing that emerges as if it were two closed sandals, with the fruit-cluster between them arranged in layers, and the tip is pointed, or it is what appears of its fruit at the first moment of its appearance."

When he mentioned what occurs only in hot lands, he said: ﴿And an extended shade﴾, meaning one that covers all time and place, so it is constantly extended, like what lies between the dawn's brightening and the rising of the sun, having no end and no termination.

Since the mention of satisfaction (al-riyy) does not necessarily imply flowing water, He said: ﴿and water poured forth﴾, meaning flowing in their dwellings without a trench, and they have no need to carry it from distant places, nor to lower buckets into a well as the people of the desert do.
When he had mentioned what came before, he generalized with his words: ﴿And fruits in abundance﴾, that is, of their kinds, their varieties, and their individual pieces.

Since they (the fruits) are not available to us except at brief times, he made clear that the matter of Paradise is otherwise, and so he said: ﴿Neither cut off﴾. And since in this world access to them may be difficult even when they exist, for something of the things, the least of which is climbing the tree or being screened off by a wall or something else, he said: ﴿nor forbidden﴾.

Since enjoyment of fruit is not complete except with comfort, He said: ﴿And raised couches﴾, meaning they are elevated in rank and high in fact, due to the abundance of their stuffing and the piling of some of them upon others (p. 209). And because they are upon thrones. Al-Baghawi related, through the chain of al-Nasa'i, from Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Their height is like the distance between the heaven and the earth, a journey of five hundred years."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 35:

Since women are called "furush" (carpets, lit. spreads), God—Exalted is He—said, repeating the pronoun in a sense other than what the mind first grasps from the outward meaning, by way of istikhdam (a figure in which one word carries two senses), emphasizing it in order to refute those who deny the resurrection: ﴿Indeed, We﴾, that is, with the power and majesty that We possess, before which nothing is great, ﴿have produced them﴾, that is, the furush whose meaning is women of the people of this world, after death, even if they are old and decrepit, by resurrection. He added to the emphasis and said: ﴿a [special] production﴾, that is, without birth, but by gathering them from the dust, just as We did with all the mukallafun (those accountable), so that they would be like their father Adam, peace be upon him, in being created from dust; thus the re-creation will be like the first creation. For this reason, all of them, upon entering Paradise, will be in his form, peace be upon him. It is also permissible that the intended meaning of "them" is the hur 'in (the wide-eyed maidens of Paradise), in which case "production" means a novel creation for which there was no prior existence.

Since the self has its most complete attention directed to exclusivity, and since the original state of a created female is that she be a virgin, he drew attention to the fact that the intended virginity is one that is lost only during intercourse and then returns, so that whenever one returns to her, one finds her a virgin. Thus He said: ﴿So We made them﴾, that is, the pure companions (al-furush al-thayyibat) and others, by Our all-encompassing greatness, ﴿virgins﴾, that is (p-210) virginity that is perpetual, because there is no change or deficiency in Paradise.

Since it was customary that a virgin suffers from her husband because of the pain that befalls her when her virginity is removed, He indicated that there is no hardship there at all, neither pain nor anything else, by His saying: ﴿loving, devoted to their husbands﴾. The word ﴿ʿuruban﴾ (plural of ʿarūb, a coquettish woman who shows affection to her husband) is the plural of ʿarūb. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': "Their understanding of the husband's desire is like the eloquence of the Arabs." Since agreement in age is more conducive to love and greater intimacy, He said: ﴿equal in age﴾, meaning of one age and one stature, ﴿girls of thirty-three years, and so are their husbands.﴾ Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': "It is taken from the play of children with dust." End of quote.

"Al-Baghawi related, through the chain of ʿAbd ibn Humayd, from al-Hasan, who said: 'An old woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah! Pray to Allah that He admit me to Paradise." He said: "O mother of so-and-so! Indeed, an old woman will not enter Paradise." So she turned away weeping. He said: "Inform her that she will not enter it while she is old. Indeed, Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, We have brought them into being﴾ [the verse]."'" Al-Tirmidhi related it from him in al-Shama'il in this mursal form. Al-Bayhaqi related it in Kitab al-Ba'th from ʿAʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her), and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat through one route from her, and through another route from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him). Our shaykh, the memorizer of his age Ibn Hajar, said: "All its routes are weak." Al-Baghawi also related, through the route of al-Tha'labi, from Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding this verse (p-211), that he said: "Your old women in this world are bleary-eyed and watery-eyed, so He will make them virgins."

Since this wondrous description calls for what the soul takes pleasure in, such that it is said: "For whom are these?"—even though this was already known beforehand—he drew attention to it with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for the companions of the right hand﴾. It is also permissible that it be connected to ﴿equal in age﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 37], explicitly affirming that they are of the same age as their husbands.

When he had finished describing what the people of this category (the people of the right hand) have, at the furthest limit of what belongs to the people of the desert, after having described what belongs to the foremost (al-sabiqun) at the highest level possible for the people of the settled towns, and since he had earlier made the comparison concerning the foremost between the earlier generations and the later ones, he did the same here and said: ﴿A multitude from the earlier generations﴾, meaning, from the companions of the right hand (ashab al-yamin).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 40:

﴿And a multitude﴾, i.e., from them, ﴿from the later ones﴾. He did not specify among them a small or large number. The apparent meaning is that the later ones are more numerous, since describing the earlier ones as numerous does not preclude the others being more numerous, so that it accords with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, this community constitutes two-thirds of the people of Paradise. They are one hundred and twenty rows, and this community accounts for eighty of them."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 41:

When he had completed the description of what the two praiseworthy categories contain, and with it the four divisions of the People of the Right Hand, namely those who are the people of the heart and the right hand, he followed it with their opposites, saying: ﴿And the companions of the left﴾, that is, the side which the Arabs regard as ill-omened (tashā'um), and by which they expressed the basest thing and the least portion of fortune. Apparently, they are the lowest of the companions of the left side (al-mash'amah), just as the companions of the right hand were below the foremost (al-sābiqūn) among the companions of the right side (al-maymanah). Then he magnified their blame and their calamity, saying: ﴿What are the companions of the left?﴾, that is, they are in a state of such wretchedness that it is worthy to be asked about.

In the commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 42:

When He had censured them and found fault with them, He mentioned their punishment, so that it would be known that the more severe category among them in wretchedness suffers the greater punishment. So He said: ﴿In scorching wind and boiling water﴾. That is, their enclosure which surrounds them is a blast from the blast of the Fire, intense, penetrating the pores, and ﴿boiling water﴾, that is, hot water reaching such a degree of heat that it melts the flesh.

When the mockery (tahakkum) in the heart, arising from the intense burning, reached a degree that exceeds description and limit, He said: ﴿And a shade﴾. Then He followed it with what explicitly states that it is mockery, so He said: ﴿of black smoke﴾, that is, a black smoke like the embers (hummam), that is, charcoal, extremely black, by what the augmentation (ziyadah) in the word conveyed and its resemblance to the form of intensification (sighat al-mubalaghah):

Since the familiar qualities of shade are coolness and relief, He negated these of it, saying: ﴿Neither cool﴾, so that it refreshes the soul, ﴿nor generous﴾, so that one may find companionship in it, take refuge in it, hope for its goodness, and rely upon it in some state by its doing what the magnanimous, forgiving person of generous character does by way of honor. Rather, it is humiliating. He called it "shade" so that the soul would find rest in it, and then He negated from it the benefit and blessing of shade, so that two burnings would combine: the despair after hope added to the burning of the black smoke, so that the distress becomes a double distress.

(p-٢١٣) When this had yielded the point that he is of the disposition of the base person, and so is the locus of heat, constriction, baseness and severity, he gave its reason with His saying: ﴿Indeed they﴾. He emphasized it, even though among them were people of hardship, because they share in finding comfort in opposing the religion by following their desires. Also, what preceded for them, compared with this punishment, was a pleasant state. He expressed it with "kānū" (they were) to indicate its deep-rootedness in them, even if their readiness for it was by innate disposition and natural temperament, so He said: ﴿they were﴾, that is, in the world. Since that was necessarily tied to continual immersion across time through the inclination of their natures, He dropped the preposition and said: ﴿before that﴾, that is, before the great matter they came to, ﴿affluent (mutrafīn)﴾, that is, in ease of living, engrossed in desires, enjoying them, firmly established in them, because their natures were strongly drawn toward them. So there resulted for them, from what was in their natures of inclining to luxury, a lack of consideration and admonition in this world, and arrogance toward those who call to God; and in the Hereafter, severity of pain, because their bodies, prepared for luxury by being accustomed to ease, are delicate, through their inclining to it and relying upon it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 46:

﴿وكانُوا﴾ That is, along with their affluence, ﴿يُصِرُّونَ﴾ that is, they persist and continue, renewing (tajdid) it constantly, owing to the natural inclination they have toward it, ﴿عَلى الحِنْثِ﴾ that is, the sin. From this is the saying of people: "The boy has reached al-hinth (ḥinth)," that is, the age of puberty (ḥulm), which is the time of being held accountable for sin. The word ḥinth is also applied to lying, to inclining toward falsehoods, to the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus), and to breaking a binding covenant.

Since this might be something customary that is excused because it is minor or occurs for a short time, He said: ﴿العَظِيمِ﴾ "the great," indicating that they make light of the great and grave ugly deeds and abominations.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 47:

When He described them as devoted to luxury and persistent in excess (isrāf), and this (state) necessarily entails idleness (baṭalah), and from idleness there results heedlessness (ghabāwah) and corruption (fasād), which necessitates wretchedness (shaqāwah), He mentioned their denial of what is not at all unclear. So He said, joining it (by ʿaṭf) to what the expression "the sin of oath-breaking (ḥinth)" conveyed, of the kind of: "So they used to swear by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that Allah would not raise up one who dies, and that the messengers are liars." ﴿And they used to say﴾, meaning: denying this repeatedly and continuously, out of coarseness or obstinacy: ﴿"When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we then indeed be raised?"﴾, meaning: "Shall we then be raised?" The operative verb has been omitted, the indication of it being "resurrected" (mab'ūthūn). It cannot govern (the interrogative) because the interrogative particle and the emphatic particle, which have the front position, carry the meaning: ﴿"When we have died"﴾, meaning: there is then no remedy left in restoring our souls in any way. ﴿"And have become"﴾, meaning: a fixed and established state, ﴿"dust and bones."﴾ Since their interrogation here was to deny that there could be any remedy in restoring our bodies or returning our souls, He repeated the interrogation to emphasize their denial and said: ﴿"Shall we indeed, then, be raised?"﴾, meaning: our resurrection is a established fact occurring at some moment of time. They used emphasis so that their denial of what is less than what is emphasized would be all the more so by way of priority.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 48:

Since their understanding was confined to what is perceptible to the senses, due to their obstinacy, and since decay, the stronger it is, the further that decayed matter seems to them from being resurrected, they said, as a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah) with a question particle, in coordination (ʿatf) with the waw in "maʿbūthūn," without emphasis by the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl): ﴿Or our forefathers?﴾ meaning: will our forefathers be raised, that is, will their resurrection come into existence after a time. They added to the remoteness already conveyed by their words ﴿the earlier ones?﴾, meaning those whose bones have decayed along with their flesh, so that they have all become dust, especially if the torrents have carried them away, scattering their dust in every direction and bearing it off in every direction.

Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir vocalized the waw with a sukun, on the basis that the coordinating particle is "aw" (or). It is also permissible (p-215) that the coordination be made upon the position (maḥall) of "inna" and its noun.

Since they had reached the utmost of coarseness, he answered their denial by affirming what they had negated, and added to it the report of their humiliation. Then he indicated the soundness of this through a rational proof (*dalil 'aqli*) for whoever can grasp it. So he said, addressing the highest of creation and the one most fitting to be addressed, because this station is not tasted in its true taste except by him, just as he alone is the one who establishes it for them and deals gently with them: ﴿Say﴾, that is, to them and to everyone like them. He emphasized it against their denial: ﴿Indeed, the former peoples﴾, those in whom you made the astonishment (*istib'ad*) at resurrection primary. He made it comprehensive by his saying ﴿and the later ones﴾, and indicated the ease of their resurrection and that it is at the utmost of certainty, alerting that their transfer through death and decay is an acquisition, not a loss.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 50:

﴿Surely they will be gathered﴾ in the passive form (ism al-maf'ul), in the place where the reckoning will take place. And since their gathering will be gradual, he expressed it with the endpoint, saying: ﴿until the appointed time﴾, that is, the time and place of ﴿a known Day﴾, that is, one specified by God, and it is of its nature that it is known by the signs it has with Him. Al-miqat (the appointed time): that by which a thing is timed, whether of time or place, i.e., a limit.

Since the time of resurrection was distant from the descent of the Qur'an, He expressed it with its particle and emphasized it because of their denial, so He said: ﴿Then﴾, meaning after the resurrection, after the gathering that comes in stages, ﴿indeed you﴾, and He confirmed what was understood from the People of the Left, that they are the lowest category of the People of the Left-hand (al-mash'ama), so He said: ﴿O you who go astray﴾, meaning those among whom heedlessness has overcome them, who do not comprehend. Then He followed that with what necessitated the judgment of their error, so He said: ﴿the deniers﴾, meaning a denial arising from error and from adhering to what only one who is deeply entrenched in denying the truth would deny. (p-216)

**[Qur'an 56:52]** ﴿Surely you will eat from a tree﴾, whose root is in the Fire.

Since the tree (*shajar*) is the source of pleasant fruits, such as the lote-tree (*sidr*) and the acacia (*talh*), He clarified it by His saying: ﴿of zaqqum﴾. That is, a thing that is at the extreme of repulsiveness and ugliness in appearance, foul smell, and harm. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qazzaz said in his comprehensive *Diwan*, and 'Abd al-Haqq in his *Wa'i*: "*al-zaqm* is drinking milk and excess in it. It is said: 'He spent the night gulping milk (*yazqumu al-laban*) in excess (*zaqman*).' From this comes *al-zaqqum* which Allah, blessed and exalted, mentioned." And the two of them said: Abu Hanifa said: "*al-zaqqum* is a tree, greyish, small-leaved, without thorns, malodorous (*dhafira*), having *ka'abir* (knobs) on its tops, and it has a flower that bees sip. Its blossom is white, the top of its leaf is very ugly, it is pasture, and its habitat is the plain."

Al-Fayruzabadi said in the *Qamus*: "In *al-dafar* with the unpointed *dal*: *al-dafar* (with vowel on the *fa*) is the occurrence of worms in food, humiliation, and stench, and it may be pronounced with a sukun. And in the pointed letter: *al-dhafar* (with vowel on the *fa*) is the intensity of the smell of the wind, like *al-dhafara*, or it is specific to the stench of the armpit, and the stench of the male's water. *Al-dhafra'* of the battalions: the sharp iron (blade). *Al-kubara* with two *damma*s and an unpointed *'ayn* and *ra'*: the knot of the stem of the crop."

And from al-Suhayli: Abu Hanifa mentioned among plants that in Yemen there is a tree called *al-zaqqum* that has no leaves, and its branches resemble most closely the heads of snakes.

Al-Baydawi said: "a tree with small leaves, malodorous, bitter, found in Tihama."

In the *Qamus*: "*al-zaqma*: the plague." And in the *Nihaya* (of Ibn al-Athir): "*fa'ul* from *al-zaqm*: intense gulping (*al-laqm al-shadid*) and excessive drinking." And Ibn al-Qatta' said: "zaqama, yazqumu zaqman: he swallowed."

It is known from the combination of these statements that it is explained as "plague" at one time and "excessive drinking" at another. From the conditions of the tree being stinking and of hideous appearance, it follows that it is a thing so disgusting that its eater is compelled to fill himself with it with great eagerness and resolve. It is known that what drives him to this, despite this repulsion, can only be at the highest levels of repulsion. Therefore the placement of His saying, as a consequence of eating, is very fitting:

Qur'an 56:53: "Then you will fill your bellies with it."

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar): ﴿فَمالِئُونَ﴾ means: a filling that is at the utmost firmness, while you are at the utmost eagerness for it, together with the great repugnance that it entails. ﴿مِنها﴾ means: from the tree; it is feminine because it is the plural of shajar (tree), or because it is a collective noun (ism jins), and since they dislike females, feminizing it (Allah knows best) adds to their aversion to it. ﴿البُطُونَ﴾ means: for a strange thing that compels you to consume this loathsome food, which is even more loathsome, with successive layers of hunger or other causes. Even if it is interpreted as what they said, that it is known to them that it is zaqqum (a tree of hellfire), that is the butter with dates, it does not harm that interpretation; rather the meaning becomes that they will fill themselves with it as one who eats of this in the world fills himself, although it is known that there is nothing good in the Fire prepared as punishment for those for whom it is prepared as punishment.

Since whoever eats much becomes intensely thirsty, and so drinks whatever he can, hoping to cool the burning of his thirst, He made the following statement a consequence of that: ﴿Then you will drink upon it﴾, that is, upon this fill (al-malī', the fullness of the belly) or the food, ﴿of the boiling water﴾, that is, the water that is at the utmost degree of heat, to the extent that its heating and boiling have been intensified.

Therefore, since their drinking of even the smallest drop of that was an utterly astonishing matter, He followed it with what is even more astonishing than it, namely the intensity of their being sated with it. So He said, as a consequence of what preceded: ﴿So you will drink﴾, meaning of it, ﴿with the drinking﴾ — shurb, with a fatha, in the reading of the majority, and with a damma for Nafi', 'Asim and Hamzah. It was also read anomalously with a kasra. All three are verbal nouns (masadir). Al-Fayruzabadi said in al-Qamus: "Shariba, like sami'a, yashrabu shurban, and it may be pronounced with three vowels. Or al-sharab is a verbal noun, while with a damma or a kasra it is a noun (ism). With a fatha, al-qawm (the people) who drink. With a kasra: the water and one's portion of it, the watering place, and the time of drinking; all of these are suitable here." ﴿Like the thirsty camels﴾, meaning the thirsty camels, because they have al-hayam, which is a disease resembling polydipsia (istisqa'), the plural of ahyam. Al-Qazzaz said: it is the plural of hayma', and al-huyam, with a damma, is a disease that afflicts camels so that they drink and are never quenched, end of quote. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*So she became like the thirsty camel, which water does not cool, and whose thirst does not end.*

It is also said that al-Hiym means the sand, into which everything poured upon it sinks away. The meaning is that they are subjected to hunger that compels them to eat, and then to thirst that compels them to drink, in this condition.

Al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar, on surah 56, verse 56:

When it was as if it had been said, "This is all their punishment," it was said, mockingly toward them and as a rebuke to them: ﴿This is their welcome gift (nuzul) on the Day of Judgment.﴾ That is, what is prepared for them at the first of their arrival, in the manner of what is prepared for a guest at the first of his arrival, as an honor to him. ﴿On the Day of Judgment﴾ means the recompense, which is the wisdom of the Resurrection. And if this is their welcome gift, then consider what will come after it in the way of one who is cared for. So consider what will be for those who are more self-sufficient than them among the obstinate ones. It is in the manner of mockery, like the saying of Abu al-Shu'ara' al-Dabbi:

*And when a tyrant with the sword would visit us as a guest,*
*We made the spears and the keen blades his welcome gift (nuzul).*

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 57:

(p-219) When He had mentioned the Event (al-Waqi'ah) and what will happen in it to the three categories, and concluded with it in a manner in which He explained its wisdom, and they were denying it, He indicated this by His saying: ﴿We﴾, meaning none other than Us, ﴿created you﴾, meaning by the greatness that belongs to Us. Perhaps this address is to the naturalist (dahriyyah) atheists among the Arabs. Since they were deniers of the resurrection (al-ba'th), they were counted as deniers of the origination (al-ibtida'), even though they were among the ones who affirm (al-mukhallisah) and acknowledge the Creator, because each of the two is necessarily linked to the other, and neither can be separated from the other. So He said: ﴿Then why﴾, meaning: as a consequence of that it is said, in threat and warning: why not, and why do you not ﴿believe﴾, meaning in the creation which you have witnessed, and about which no one disputes with Us, so that you would believe in what is not distinguished from it except in that it is more difficult within the customary course of your affairs, namely the re-creation (al-i'adah), so that you would act as slaves act toward their masters, so that your condition would be the condition of one who believes that he is a created being under the lordship of another (marbub).

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 58:

When He had urged them to affirm (taṣdīq) by way of reasoning from their own creation, and resurrection is nothing other than transforming them from a decayed form into the form they had been in before, He consequently linked their denial of it, despite their affirmation of creation, to their failure to reflect on the transformation of forms in its details. Or He linked it to the words of one who might say, from among the people of natural philosophy (ṭabā'i' — the natural philosophers): "We were created from a drop that came into being through an inherent heat." So He said: ﴿Have you considered?﴾, meaning: tell Me, have you seen, with the eye or with insight (baṣīrah), that We created you, so that this would guide you to the fact that We are able to bring you back just as We were able to originate you? Then ﴿you have considered﴾ [what you emit] — meaning: what you pour forth (tumnūn, from manā, to emit) — from the drops which are semen (maniyy) into the wombs through sexual intercourse.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 59:

Since the consideration is with the effect (al-musabbab) and not with the cause (al-sabab), he drew attention to this by renewing the denial [p. 220], to alert that they, although they acknowledged that He alone is the Originator, their denial of resurrection entails their denial of this. So He said: ﴿Is it you who create it?﴾, meaning, do you bring it into existence, determined in the state of proportion and wisdom it has, after its creation from the form of a drop of semen to the form of a clinging clot, then from the form of a clot to the form of a lump of flesh, then from it to the form of bones and sinews, ﴿or is it We [alone]?﴾ And since the context was to establish the point against the deniers, he mentioned the information that is understood from the context in a manner that conveyed that the implied meaning is: "Or are you the creators of it, or are We?" So He said: "Rather, We are ﴿the Creators﴾", meaning, that this attribute is established for Us. Thus the verse is of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which each of two paired elements omits what the other supplies): He first mentioned *taklaqun* (تَخْلُقُونَ, "you create") as evidence for the omission of its like for Him, the Exalted, in the second part, and He mentioned the noun (al-ism) in the second part as evidence for the omission of its like for them in the first part. The secret of this is that He mentioned what is more suitable to their actions, of what indicates the occurrence of renewal, even if for some time, and what is more fitting to His attributes, the Exalted, of what indicates permanence and continuity.

Since the answer is "You alone are the Creator," and the naturalist (al-ṭabīʿī, i.e., the proponents of natures, *ahl al-ṭabāʾiʿ*) might say that the heat that ferments the sperm-drop necessitates it, and since the differing terms of life-spans, despite equality in the name of life, are among the great proofs of complete power over causing to perish and causing to originate by choice, which nullifies the claim of the people of natures and refutes them, he confirmed this proof with His words: ﴿We﴾, that is, by the greatness that is ours and not another's, ﴿have decreed﴾, that is, a great decree (p-221) which no one other than Us can annul in any part of it, ﴿among you﴾, that is, all of you, not leaving anyone among you without a share of it, ﴿death﴾, that is, We have made it obligatory at a known measure for each person, which he cannot exceed. So We shortened the life of this one, though he may have been at the peak of bodily strength and sound temperament. Even if all creation gathered to prolong his life, they could not delay it for a moment. And We lengthened the life of that one, though he may be at the lowest point of bodily weakness and disordered temperament. Even if they all colluded to shorten it by the blink of an eye, they would be unable to do so. You acknowledge that He, glorified is He, arranged His acts according to the requirements of perfection, power and consummate wisdom. If the purpose of death were merely subjugation, it would be a deficiency, since it encompasses the rich and the poor, the oppressor and the oppressed. And making man immortal would have been more fitting and more wise. Therefore its purpose is other than mere subjugation, and it is the prompting toward excellence in works for the Subjugator, out of fear of being presented before Him and being called to account in His presence, then the transfer to the abode of recompense; and the elevation to the sciences of which the body is a veil, such as distinguishing the wicked from the good and knowing the measures of reward and punishment, and other things that people of understanding perceive.

Since the outcome of death is that it is a change of the form that was into another, and whoever is able to transform a form into one thing is able to transform it into another thing similar to that thing, he said: ﴿And We are not﴾, that is, with the greatness that is ours, and he emphasized the negation, saying: ﴿outdone﴾, that is, by death, nor incapable, nor overcome.

"upon that We change your likenesses with a great change, and We create you in what you do not know." Let me translate carefully.

Translation:

﴿upon that We change﴾ a great change ﴿your likenesses﴾, i.e., your forms and persons, in accordance with what preceded in al-Shura that the likeness (mithl) in origin is the very thing itself, ﴿and We create you﴾, i.e., a new creation after the change of your essences, ﴿in what you do not know﴾ (p-222). For some of them are eaten by beasts of prey, fish, or birds, so their bodies come to be formed from that; and some of them turn to dust, and perhaps a plant grows from it, which is eaten by animals, and so their bodies are formed from it; and perhaps their dust becomes part of the minerals of the earth, such as gold, silver, iron, stone, and the like. His words, exalted is He, allude to this: ﴿Say: Be stones or iron﴾ [al-Isra: 50] ﴿or a creation [of what is greater in your breasts]﴾ [al-Isra: 51], to the end of the verse. Or the meaning, as al-Baghawi said, is: We bring a creation like you in your place, and We create you in forms You do not know, that is, by changing your attributes and forms into other forms through transformation (maskh). And whoever is able to do that is able to restore you.

Since the sense is "Indeed you have known the second creation, the seminal one," he attached to it his saying, emphatically, as a reminder that when they acted contrary to what they knew, they were as if they denied this knowledge: ﴿And indeed you have known﴾, that is, O Arabs, ﴿the first creation﴾, the creation from dust of your father Adam, upon him be prayers and peace; or the creation from flesh of your mother Hawwa (Eve), peace be upon her, since there was then no natural cause requiring it, for otherwise the like would have been found after that. And the seminal creation is known to you. Each of these is a transformation from one thing into another. So the One whose power over that you have witnessed, is He not able to transform you, after you have become dust, back into the form you were in at first? For this reason, He made a consequence of what preceded it his saying: ﴿Then why will you not remember?﴾, that is, why not, and why do you not? ﴿Remember﴾ with a great remembrance, which you would find distasteful for yourselves, although in it there is some obscurity, which the idgham (assimilation) hints at, in that the thing blamed for it is unseen. Likewise (p-223) some of what was used as analogy, that whoever is able to these forms of origination is able to bring back, indeed it is easier in the course of your customary experience.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 63:

Since their knowledge of the matter of plants, which is the greatest sign for the resurrection of the dead, is greater than their knowledge of everything that has passed, and since their action of tilling and casting the seed [into the soil] is most similar to intercourse and the casting of the sperm-drop, for which reason a woman is called a field (harth), he connected it to what has passed as a consequence of it, saying in reproach to them: ﴿Have you considered?﴾ That is: tell me, have you seen, with the eye or with insight, what We have drawn your attention to, and what preceded it, so that as a result of your attention to that, you have seen ﴿what you till﴾? That is: you renew its tilling continuously by preparing its land for the seed and casting the seed into it.

Since they do not claim the power to make things grow in any way, and the One who has power over it has power over everything, while they hold beliefs about the matter of resurrection that lead to disparaging His power, He repeated the rebuke against them and said: ﴿Do you cause it to grow, or are We the ones who cause it to grow?﴾ That is, do you make it sprout after you have cast the seed into the ground and guard it until it becomes wealth? ﴿Or are We the sowers?﴾ Here "We" is specific, and he affirmed what had passed by mentioning the report that is known from the context, so he said: ﴿the sowers﴾, that is, the ones who make it grow and the ones who guard it. So the verse is of the type of *ihtibak* (interlocking ellipsis), just like its counterpart verse shortly before it, exactly the same.

(p-224) When the answer was decisive, "Are you alone the one who did that?" [He said], clarifying, since no one else had sown it, that the perfect doer is the one who protects what he has made from whatever would spoil it, and whoever, if he wished to spoil it, no one could prevent. ﴿Had We willed﴾, i.e., had We dealt with you by the attribute of greatness. He emphasized this because their conduct was that of one who feels secure from such a thing, while they were in extreme disbelief that their crop could perish as they had sown it. Or it is because food is more important and greater than drink, for it is the basis of sustaining the body, while drink follows it. So He said: ﴿We would have made it﴾, i.e., with that greatness, ﴿debris (ḥuṭāman)﴾, i.e., broken and crumbled, with no grain in it, either before it sprouted, so that it would not accept growing, or after it, through excessive cold, destroying heat, or otherwise, so that it could not be benefited from. ﴿Then you would remain﴾, i.e., you would remain because of that, at the time of great occupations and at every time, abandoning everything that concerns you, ﴿amazed (tafakkahūn)﴾. In the Qamus (the dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī) it says: "Fakkahahum bi-mulaḥ al-kalām" means he amused them with witty speech, and "fakiha" (in the pattern of "faraḥa") "fakahan," so he is "fakih" and "fākih," meaning good of spirit, or one who speaks to his companions so that they laugh. From this comes "ta'ajjaba" (to marvel), like "tafakkaha." "Al-tafākuh" is joking, and "tafakkaha" is to regret. "Al-ufkūkah" is wonder. Ibn Barjān said: "The fakih is one who wavers in speech, going in every direction with it," end of quote.

You would remain constantly regretting your stubbornness or your sins that caused that loss, or marveling, or talking about it, and you would not turn aside to occupy yourselves with anything else, as you do when you encounter things that delight you, which are extremely wondrous, pleasant, and agreeable. For this reason He expressed what is meant by remaining continually with the word "ẓalla," whose meaning is "he remained during the day," indicating the abandonment of the occupations that concern a person, whose place is the day, and a person is prevented from most of what concerns him in speech because of this great calamity. He omitted one of the two lams of "ẓalla" and the tā' of the taf'ul pattern from "tafakkaha," indicating (p-225) the weakness of those afflicted in defending themselves in their survival and in their speech during their weak state. The fact that the omitted letter is the middle radical of the verb, which is the medial one, indicates the tearing out of the heart, the rupture of the belly, and great subjugation. So none of them has any power to resist this calamity in any way, nor to cool the burning in the chest and the fear of poverty that has seized him, except by complaining of his hopes to one who knows that there is no harm or benefit in his hand. Perhaps that is a sign that it is His habit, glorified be He, that relief comes near in the hardships of this world, so that a person is able to give thanks, with no excuse left for him in neglecting it. The meaning is that you, despite the abundance of your experience of relief after hardship, soon despair when the trial first strikes you, so you turn to much complaining, and the abundance of past experiences will never benefit you in bringing about blessings.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 66:

When He mentioned their tafakkuh (exclamation of wonder and regret, and also enjoyment, a word that is one of the "opposites," i.e. a single word with two contrary meanings), and tafakkuh was applied both to what was mentioned, namely wonder and regret, and to luxuriating in comfort, al-Kisa'i said: it is one of the words of opposite meanings (al-adhdad). The Arabs say: "tafakkahtu," meaning "I lived in comfort," and "tafakkahtu," meaning "I grieved." By his saying, as a quotation of their tafakkuh, ﴿Indeed we﴾, he made the intended meaning clear, and he emphasized it to inform of the severity of their distress, [so] he said: ﴿are laden with debt﴾, meaning: we are devoted to misfortune and constantly bound to ruin, torment and destruction, because the sustenance we had has been destroyed; or: we are deprived (made to suffer loss) through the cost of what we spent, from which no benefit was gained. The reading of Abu Bakr from 'Asim, with the interrogative form, is for denying this event, deeming it grave, and expressing wonder at it. It serves to alert that, because of the severity of their agitation over that occurrence, they are wavering: at times they are certain of despair and misfortune, and at times they doubt it and attribute the matter to the badness of their own conduct, and their retraction (idrabuhum) indicates this: (p-226)

Translation:

﴿Rather, we are﴾ — that is, exclusively — ﴿deprived﴾; that is, others have been deprived by Him, and He is the One whose decree cannot be turned back. So there is no share for us in earning. For if the sower were among those who have a share, his crop would have prospered.

Al-Fayruzabadi (the author of al-Qamus) said: al-gharam means excessive attachment (wuluww), constant harm, ruin and punishment. Al-gharamah is that which must be paid. Harama him means he prevented him. Al-mahrum is one who is prevented from good, or whose wealth does not grow, and al-muhraf (with the ra vowelled with fatha) is one who is prevented from good and who hardly ever earns. Al-Asfahani said in his tafsir: al-mahrum is the opposite of al-marzuq, and al-marzuq is al-majrud (with the jim), which is the one who is granted good fortune.

When He made them stand before His power over the crops, despite the existence of their causes, and brought them forward with force toward Him, and since it might have been that some confusion arose [in their minds], because they had some share of causation in the matter in general, He followed it with a warning about His power to dispose of its cause, which is water. They have no causal role at all in any part of its affair. So He said, as a consequence of what this admonition conveyed to them, reminding them of the blessing of drink, which food requires: ﴿Have you considered﴾, meaning: tell Me, have you seen, with the eye or with insight, what We have alerted you to of what has passed regarding food and other things? ﴿Have you considered the water﴾. And since some water is not drinkable, and the blessing lies more greatly in what is drunk, He described it with a description that made a description of its sweetness unnecessary, and clarified the locus of the blessing from which there is no escape, saying: ﴿which you drink﴾.

Since its origin is in the direction of height, He said, rebuking them and establishing (the fact) for them: ﴿Is it you who sent it down﴾. And since "sending down" (inzal) may be applied to the mere bringing into existence of a precious thing, and the cloud by its habit passes along with the wind and hardly remains, He expressed (it) with His saying, affirming the direction of height and drawing attention to the place of the blessing in its (the rain's) continuance until the benefit from it is fully obtained: ﴿from the rain-cloud﴾, that is, the cloud, the full and praised one, whose nature is to hasten onward. Al-Isfahani said: "It is said: specifically the white cloud, and it is the sweetest of water." ﴿Or are We the ones who send it down﴾, that is, exclusively. He emphasized it by mentioning the predicate, though it does not need to be mentioned in the basic meaning, so He said: ﴿the ones who send it down﴾, that is, to it, as mercy [for you] and kindness toward you, by making your life pleasant, through the station of greatness that We possess, whose nature is pride, majesty, and indifference to anything. And the verse is of the (rhetorical device of) ihtibak, like what passed in the two preceding verses, exactly the same.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 70:

When the answer was: "You alone did that, despite being independent of creation, by virtue of Your mercy and the perfection of Your essence and attributes," He said, reminding them of another blessing: ﴿If We willed﴾, that is: while it is being sent down and is far off, before it can be benefited from. And since the turning of water into [salt] is more common than the turning of plants into debris, He did not emphasize it for this reason, and to alert that the listeners, since the demonstration of complete power had already passed, had come to be among those who acknowledge it. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We have made it﴾, that is, in accordance with what the attributes of greatness require, ﴿salty﴾, that is: bitter, burning salt, as if in the bowels there is the blaze of a kindled fire, so it does not quench thirst nor produce any plant that can be benefited from. And since this is something that cannot be accepted by denial, (p-228) he made the following a consequence of it, by way of rebuke and urging: ﴿Then why do you not give thanks?﴾, that is: why not, and why would you not renew thanks continuously by using the powers that this water has granted you in obedience to the One who brought it into existence for you, enabled you to use it, made it agreeable to your natures, desirable to your souls, and beneficial to you in everything you see.

When fire was a cause for the element that holds water, so that it drips and trickles, just as water was a cause for splitting the earth to produce crops, and no created being has the power to reach anything except through some kind of cause, He followed it with the fire as He had followed the crops with water. This was both for that reason and to show the power over what has no cause created by any creature in the lower world, just as the sending down of water was free of their (human) customs in the heights. So He said, drawing a conclusion from what preceded, as an alert that He had qualified them to reflect on His creations and to consider the wonders of His signs. He said: ﴿Have you considered?﴾, that is, tell me, have you seen with your eyes and your insight what has preceded, so that you have seen ﴿the fire﴾? And since the intended meaning is a specific fire, one that makes them stand upon the completeness of His power and reveals this to them in a clear unveiling through the bringing of things out of their opposites, He said: ﴿that you kindle﴾, that is, you draw it out from the firestick and so you kindle with it, whether the firestick is dry or green, after it had been hidden within it. Whoever has not tested this would not suppose that there is any fire in it at all. This is like the tawriya (an allusion in which one thing is shown while another is meant), in which something appears and something else is intended. Then after that hiddenness it passes to great manifestation, increasing dominion and evident majesty, burning everything it touches, even that from which it came out. The Arabs are the people most knowledgeable about the firestick. They cut a branch from the tree of al-markh (Rhus/Mrakh tree) and another from al-'afar (a tree of the same kind), and rub one against the other, and fire sparks from them. Fire is in every tree, but al-markh and al-'afar were singled out because sparks are easily struck from them. They have said: "There is fire in every tree, and al-markh and al-'afar have gained glory."

Now that this is among the wonders of creation, he repeated the affirmation and the rebuke to draw attention to it, saying: ﴿Is it you who produced it﴾, i.e., invented, brought into existence, deposited, gave life to, nurtured, and caused it to occur, ﴿its tree﴾, i.e., the markh and the 'affar, from which you make the firestriker (zind) from which the fire is drawn, and you lodged the fire in them, mixed with water, which is its opposite, and you concealed it in that tree, such that neither of the two overcomes the other, despite their opposition, so that one prevails over the other until it annihilates and destroys it. ﴿Or are We﴾, i.e., exclusively, and he emphasized it with his saying: ﴿the producers﴾, i.e., of it, by what We possess of greatness in that form. So whoever is able to [bring into being] the fire, which is the driest of all green trees, along with the watery moisture in it that is opposed to it in its nature, is more able to restore freshness and softness to the dust of the body, which was once soft and tender, then dried up and decayed. This verse is of the method of ihtibak, in the same manner as in its sister verses, identically.

Since the answer was decisively "You alone," He said, indicating that and calling attention to the greatness of this report: ﴿We﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿have made it﴾ in accordance with what Our greatness requires, and He placed first among its benefits what is more fitting to the context of resurrection, which is its proper setting, so He said: ﴿a reminder﴾, that is, something you remember and by which you remember with a great and magnificent remembrance of all that We have told you about resurrection and the punishment of the great Fire, and the tree of Zaqqum that grows in it, and other things which We illuminate for those of insight and understanding among the sciences. Ibn Burjan said: the analogy is the striking of a firestarter from the tree, and the firestarter is an analogy for the Cry upon them, and an analogy for His creating bodies is an analogy for His creating the tree of fire. Through its creation from the tree one is reminded of the creation of life in bodies, and through its creation from its unseen source one is reminded that the great Fire is in the unseen realm beyond what we witness, and this is among the effects of its existence in the air. End of quote. He also attached to it, glorified is He, many of the means of livelihood that are indispensable, so that it would be a constant reminder to them of what they kindle, present always, making them more fit to take warning. ﴿And a provision﴾, that is, a creation, a sustenance, a maintenance, a benefit, and a conveyance to the purpose intended from illumination, warming, cooking, dissolving, melting, hardening, calcining, and the fleeing of wild beasts, and other things; the meaning is that it is a cause of all of that. ﴿For the desert dwellers﴾, that is, the hungry whose stomachs have become empty, from poverty and wealth alike, who descend upon the barren land (al-qiwa'). Al-qiwa' with a kasra and a mad (qifa') means the empty, desolate, widely spaced wastelands far from settlement. Every human being is prepared for qiwa', so he is described by it even if he is not currently in that state. Al-Razi said: "aqwa" is among the antonyms: it means he became rich and he became poor. Abu Hayyan said: these four which Allah Most High mentioned and made them aware of concerning the matter of their creation and what sustains their livelihood, of food and drink, and fire is among the greatest proofs of resurrection, since in it there is a transition from one thing to another and the bringing forth of one thing from another, and for this reason He commanded at its end to glorify Him. End of quote.

When He, glory be to Him, had pointed in these verses to the wonders of His power and the marvels of His craftsmanship, beginning with the sowing and ending with the fire and the tree, and had made obligatory what He had drawn attention to, namely remembrance of these things and reflection upon their affairs, [that they are] among the causes of what precedes them, and that He is a cause of them because He is a cause of them, in order to establish what they are for, and the totality of that was an allusion to the four elements, Ibn Burjan said: "Except that water and earth are for the creation of the foundations, while the characteristics and attributes belong to air and fire." And all of that, in every aspect, was a dazzling matter. He indicated the increase in its greatness by commanding tanzih (declaring Him free of imperfection), as a consequence of what that conveyed. So He said, turning away from those who might be touched by denial and turning toward the most noble of His creation, as an indication that no one other than him understands this station as it should be understood, nor acts upon it as it should be acted upon: ﴿So glorify﴾, that is, bring about the great tanzih, free of every trace of deficiency, such as abandoning the resurrection and other things, especially after these proofs have reached the level of the perceptible. It is the glorification of one who marvels at the signs of His power, which indicate the limitlessness of His greatness; the glorification of thankfulness to Him, of exalting and magnifying Him; and the declaring of Him free of what the deniers say, and a marvelling at them, following the example of all that is in the heavens and the earth. Among the most wondrous of this is that He has subjected to us in this abode Hell.
