Ibn Burjan said: "He made from it, by the heat of the sun, gardens, fruits, fruit-bearing trees, crops and means of livelihood." (p. 232)

Since the magnifying of the Name is more firmly established in the magnifying of the One named, He said: ﴿in the name﴾, that is, invoking the name of ﴿your Lord﴾, that is, the One who has been bountiful to you after nurturing you, with this greatest exposition, through what He has singled you out with, which He has given to no one else but you. They wrote the connecting alif (alif al-wasl) here because its occurrence is not as frequent as its occurrence in the basmala, and they omitted it from there because of how often the basmala occurs. Their practice is brevity and reducing what is abundant once its meaning is known, and this is well known and not unknown. The retention of what is retained of its forms, which do not occur often, is evidence of its omission from there. Likewise, the alif is not omitted with any letter other than the bā' in the name of Allah, nor with the bā' in names other than the Name of Majesty, for the reason mentioned earlier.

Since the context calls for magnification, He said: ﴿the Mighty﴾, who has filled all the worlds with His greatness, so that nothing in them is without being filled with His greatness, in transcendence above being touched by any trace of deficiency or missing any perfection. Al-Qushayri said: These signs which He, glory be to Him, enumerated are a preparation for following the path of inference, and as in the report: "An hour of reflection is better than sixty years of worship." This is the contemplation to which Allah has drawn attention.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 56, verse 75:

Since the splendour of the blessings that appeared in this surah, in their varied forms, across both abodes was so great, and since it began with the blessing of the Hereafter because it is the outcome, and then indicated it through His favour in this world, it served as a reminder of the blessings so that they would be thanked, and as an indication of the outcome so that it would be remembered. In every case it is brought to mind, so that it is not denied. The indication thus reached a degree clearer than what is perceived by the senses and brighter than the sun. Alongside these magnificent matters [p. 233] it was in a form that rendered all creatures unable to produce its like in every respect. As for its answer to their confusion and obstinacy, it corresponds to that in a correspondence such that nothing could be like it. It adds to that what God wills of knowledge, without leaving any ambiguity. As for its vocabulary, it is the utmost in the sublimity of its words, the grace of its letters, and the gathering of meanings, which indicates that no other word can take the place of any one of its words at all. As for its composition, each of its words is most fitting in its place, such that if any of them were moved forward or delayed, the intended meaning in that context would be disrupted according to that situation. As for the order of its sentences, verses and narratives, in their beginnings and endings, it is like the composition of its words: every sentence is arranged with what precedes it, like the arrangement of a unique pearl in a well-woven, finely ordered necklace, because each is either a cause of what follows, or a proof, or a completion in some respect among the excellent aspects, in a manner that delights the hearer and is noble in its veil, so that it is sweeter in his mouth and clearer, after his tasting, in its arrangement and in all his knowledge. Thus the establishment of all that it informs of is in a way where there is no hesitation or pause in believing its beauty. It is established that God, exalted is He, sent the one who brought this Qur'an, ﷺ, with guidance and with truth, not that He gave him everything that is fitting for him. So He gave him wisdom (*hikmah*), which is decisive proofs and their correct application in their proper ways, and fine admonition (*al-mawʿizah al-hasanah*), which is matters that soften hearts and illuminate breasts, and argumentation (*al-mujadalah*) that is in the best of methods, in a miraculous arrangement that necessitates faith. Thus whoever heard it [p. 234] and did not believe was left with nothing from the impossible positions except to say: "This eloquence is not for the manifestation and establishment of the claim, but for the strength of the claimant's rhetorical power and his ability to construct proofs, shape speech and vary the modes of discourse." He knows that he is prevailing by the strength of his argument, not by the clarity of his message, just as one of two debaters, when he is defeated, may say to his opponent: "You know that the truth is with me, but you belittle me and do not do me justice." At that point the opponent has no answer except to swear oaths, binding ones from which there is no escape, that he is not obstinate and that he is fair. He only resorts to oaths because if he brought another proof he would be exposed to the same thing, and would say: "You have overcome me in this by the strength of your argument and your power to marshal proofs with the eloquence of your speech." Therefore, when the Prophet ﷺ silenced them, they used to say: "He wants to show superiority over us," in matters where they knew the opposite. Nothing was left but oaths, so God sent down various kinds of oaths after the great proofs. For this reason the verses increased at the ends of the Qur'an, and especially in the last seven, even more. Therefore, He made His saying ﴿So I swear not﴾ follow from these wondrous proofs and decisive demonstrations, with the negating *lā* affirmed. This may be either as an emphatic device, by negating the opposite of what the oath affirms, so that the speech combines affirming the meaning reported and negating its opposite; or it may be understood as implying: this situation, because of its greatness and their denial of it, deserves that [p. 235] one swear by something greater than this, given its greatness, for whoever has knowledge. And God knows best.

Since the preceding discourse concerned the water which God, glorified is He, made a gathering of visible worldly blessings, and He arranged the sending of the rains according to a method He devised and a law He perfected, and made the sending down of the Qur'an in separate stars and flashing, brilliant lightnings, He said: ﴿by the places of the stars﴾, that is, by the falling places of the Qur'anic groups, which are luminous, beneficial, and life-giving to hearts, and by their descent, upon which many great effects are based, and by the times and places of that and its circumstances; and by the setting places of the stars and their risings, their times and places, in His management as you see of perfected craftsmanship and precisely formed action, which by the setting of the stars indicates the power to fold up after spreading out and to annihilate after bringing into being; and by their rising, which shows that they are compelled towards it, like something falling from high to low that owns nothing of itself, because of His power to bring into being after annihilation; and by the effects of the rains in a similar manner, more clearly than that. And other indications beyond these, which words cannot contain and which lengthy allusions fall short of reaching in their heights. For such great meanings and mighty matters, He placed a parenthetical insertion (*iʿtiraḍ*) between the oath and its answer, and within that insertion another between the qualified and its qualifier, as an emphasis on the speech and a jolt to penetrating understandings, alerting that the matter is great and the affair is weighty and momentous. So He said, clarifying it with emphasis out of mercy to the servants, by indicating that they proceeded with what contradicts what they know of our greatness, so they were counted as not knowing:

**(p. 236)** [This] oath, following this method, ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you knew.﴾ That is: if knowledge were renewed for you at some time, you would know that it is ﴿mighty﴾. His swearing it to us, while we are of lesser worth and weaker affair, is to make known the mercy He has, and from its greatness is that He does not leave us aimless. All of this is so that He may correct our souls by following His command and halting at His prohibition.

Ibn Barjan said: "Among His perfect craftsmanship, exalted is His majesty, in His creation and His wisdom in His creatures, is that He made for every star of the celestial spheres that sets a rising star, called in relation to the setting one its watcher (raqib), without delay. This is what is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman: 17] ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 18]. This comprises the sun, the moon and the stars, and these are the stars of the lunar mansions (manazil al-qamar), whose number is twenty-eight mansions, apart from those which the sun conceals. Thus twenty-nine mansions are complete, which the moon overlooks. Sometimes it is hidden for one night and sometimes for two nights. The moon descends into these mansions, one mansion each night, until it completes them [for the completion] of the month. As for the sun, it remains in each mansion [of them] for thirteen days, except for the direction in which it remains for fourteen days. The sun's arrival in these places is called, then the rising of the mansion that follows it, because this one is its watcher, a nawʾ (a star whose rising is associated with rain)." End of quotation. He means that whoever reflects on these wisdoms knows the greatness of this oath. Abu al-Hakam expanded on this matter and explained what it contains of wondrous blessings.

Then he said: "And [God] bestows, by opening His mercy as He wills, so He sends down [from the sky] blessed water with which He breaks the bitter cold (zamharir) by moistening it, and cools the heat of the blaze (saʿir) by balancing it. He divided the year into four seasons, in which He completed His command on earth with its blessings and the measuring of its sustenance (aqwat), [He said: and He blessed therein and measured therein its sustenance] in four days." Then he said: "He made this world, in this consideration, the lesser garden (al-jannah al-sughra). Had He completed the division in this manner, it would be complete in consideration: its lightening of the scorching heat (fayh) and its illumination of the zamharir. The saʿir is the lesser Hell (jahannam al-sughra)."

Having completed the oath in this glorious manner, He answered it with His words, emphasizing [what was] the apparent denial on their part: ﴿Indeed, it﴾, that is, the Qur'an, whose meaning the stars made understood through the generality of their meanings, ﴿is indeed a Qur'an﴾ [i.e.] comprehensive, easy, near, understandable, clarifying the obscure, possessing glorious kinds, ﴿noble﴾, in which the varieties of His favor, glory be to Him, appear regarding the subtle matters of this world and the sublime matters of both abodes, through what it mentions in this surah and what precedes it, of the setting right of the livelihood and the afterlife. So it is utterly noble, free from every trace of deficiency, baseness, and lowliness. Among its nobility is that it came from the Sovereign Most High to the best of creation through the mediation of the Spirit of Holiness (Ruh al-Qudus), and in the tongue of the Arabs [whose tongue all the sects agree is the most eloquent of tongues, and in a manner that rendered the Arabs incapable].

When he had mentioned the meaning, he mentioned the place of the composition (al-nazm), which indicates it by a term that indicates the very composition itself, and so he said: ﴿In a Book﴾, that is, in writing and in something written, collected in a manner that is at the utmost of firmness, ﴿well-guarded﴾, that is, it is in a protected covering, because of its precious and exalted station: in the heavens, in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz); on earth, in the noble breasts (of men); and in the lines, in the honored and purified mushafs; preserved, along with that, from alteration and substitution.

Since what is described is such that a flaw may befall it that would distress its attendants, He said: ﴿None touches it﴾, meaning the Book in which it is written, which is more general than whether it is in the heavens or on the earth, or the Qur'an, or the written copy of it, let alone handling it. ﴿Except the purified﴾, meaning the pure ones who have been intensely purified, who are the chiefs of the noble angels. The emissary (al-safir) with it was none other than them, and God did not facilitate its preservation except for His purest servants, nor did He make its meaning known except to the most noble of its custodians and the purest of them in heart. Among the generality of what the wording bears in meaning, given that it is the speech of the One who knows all things, is that it carries no word except that it is intended for it: that it is forbidden to be touched by one who is not in a state of utmost purity, by being free of the two impurities, the major (al-akbar) and the minor (al-asghar). On this reading, it is a negation with the force of a prohibition, and this is more emphatic. Al-Baghawi said: this is the view of most of the people of knowledge. It has been narrated with a chain through Abu Mus'ab, from Malik, from Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Amr ibn Hazm, that "in the document which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote for Amr ibn Hazm, may Allah be pleased with him, was: 'None should touch the Qur'an except one who is pure.'" By it is meant the codex (al-mushaf), by way of proximity (lil-jiwar), as in the prohibition against travelling with the Qur'an into the land of the enemy. Among what the expression by touching (al-lams) also admits is that none should recite it with his tongue except one who is pure. (p-٢٣٩) If the intended meaning is ritual impurity from sexual intercourse (al-janabah), then the prohibition is for ruling (lil-hurmah) or for the more perfect state (lil-akmal).

When He had mentioned that from which it is protected, He followed it with its nobility, through the nobility of its origin and its sending down, in a state that is at the utmost of greatness, naming it by the verbal noun (ism al-masdar) for emphasis (al-mubalaghah), and because this verbal noun is the most prevalent of its states; for this reason this name came to predominate over it: ﴿a revelation (tanzil)﴾, meaning its arrival to you by gradualness (al-tadrij) according to events, and by bringing it near to understandings, deliberation (al-ta'anni), and elevation (al-tarqiyah) from one state to another and from wisdoms, through the mediation of the Messengers from among the angels.

And since this is in the utmost of ease and facility, He mentioned of its attributes what suits it, saying: ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning from the Creator, the All-Knowing of their nurturing (tarbiyah).

When the description of this great Book made clear what, by itself, establishes its perfection, which minds cannot fully grasp, and suffices to produce submission to belief in it, how much more so when it is what reason judges and decides that anything other than it is corrupt, and how much more so when it is something a person can recall the like of within himself, He marvelled at their making it a cause for denying the Resurrection. A person who considers the states of his own self is sufficient in that for certainty about it. So He said, denouncing with wonder: ﴿Is it then of this discourse﴾. Since man is fond of the blessings renewed for him, even minor ones, how much more so when it is the highest of blessings, He said: ﴿the discourse﴾, meaning the one whose lofty attributes have preceded, and whose sending down to you is renewed time after time. ﴿You﴾, meaning you, the Arabs, the eloquent, the fluent and the rhetoricians, ﴿are mudhinun﴾ [p. 240], meaning liars and hypocrites because of it, showing the opposite of what you conceal, that it is a lie, while you know its truth from the excellence of its meanings and your inability to match its arrangement and structures. You say, "If we willed, we could say the like of this." Yet all your actions contradict this, for you endure the clash of swords and the embrace of deaths, and you bring nothing that opposes it, that rivals any part of it, or that contradicts it. Or, O believers, you are lenient toward whoever denies it and reviles its heights, or who seeks, even in a hidden way, to undo any of its bonds, out of negligence toward it, and you are not firm in dealing with it or in glorifying its matter, until you would be harder than iron.

In al-Qamus he said: dahana means he was hypocritical. al-mudahanah (compromise, flattery) means showing the opposite of what one conceals, like idhan (concealed hypocrisy) and deceit. Al-Baghawi, may God have mercy on him, said: it is idhan, which is acting inwardly contrary to what is shown outwardly. Al-Razi said: the difference between mudara (conciliation) and mudahanah lies in intention. Whatever is done for a purpose other than God is mudahanah, and whatever is done for a matter connected to religion is mudara. Ibn Burjan said: idhan and mudahanah are softness in matters, negligence, and inclining to overlook, and it ends.

On this reading, it is a rebuke against one who hears someone speak about the Qur'an in an unseemly way and then does not openly oppose him with enmity. The people of ittihad (the doctrine of unity of existence), such as Ibn 'Arabi al-Ta'i, author of the Fusus, and Ibn al-Farid, author of the Ta'iyyah, are the first to whom this verse is directed. They spoke about the Qur'an in a way that nullifies the religion entirely, root and branch, untying it knot by knot. They are therefore the most harmful of people to this religion. Whoever interprets for them, defends them, or thinks well of them, in opposition to the consensus of the community, is in a state more impure than theirs, for his aim is to preserve their words, the most corrupting of them for Islam, without any benefit in preserving them in any way whatsoever.

Since this Qur'an is charged with securing the happiness of both abodes, God Most High said: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny﴾, meaning: your share [and portion] and all that you benefit from this Book, which is all of your benefit, ﴿that you deny﴾, meaning you actually bring about the reality of denial in the past and the present, and you renew that at every time, with regard to it and to the noble matters it guides to, which are everything worthy of being believed, and you describe it with contradictory attributes. Among that is what it guides to, namely that there is no agent except God Most High. So when He sends down rain on you that provides for you, you say: "This is due to the nawʾ (the rising or setting of a particular lunar mansion) of such-and-such," believing in that nawʾ's influence, whereas it is from God Most High. Thus you made the recompense for provision, and the expression of gratitude for it, denial.

Ibn Burjan said: "And you make My provision to you [consisting of] a great Qur'an I sent down, a great speech I revealed, a light of faith I clarified, a radiance of certainty I manifested, and what I sent down from the sky of blessings I decreed, and winds I released, and clouds I assembled, you make, in place of gratitude for that, denial."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 83:

When He denounced them for this denial and marveled at them for this astonishment, in that they would attribute an act to other than Him or deny a report from Him, He consequently stated, as a confirmation that there is no doer besides Him: ﴿Why then,﴾ and "fa-lawla" is a particle that conveys a demand accompanied by rebuke, reproach and censure (p-242) with the meaning of "why not" and "why do you not." ﴿When it reaches﴾ [i.e.,] the soul from you and from others at the time of dying, it was elided without mention, because the speech indicates it with clear indication ﴿the throat (al-hulqum)﴾. It is the passage of food in the throat, and "al-halq" (the throat) is the place through which food and drink pass, which is well known. So al-hulqum is the nearest part of the throat to the direction of the tongue, because the mim is for the point of complete cessation of the sound.

Surah 56, verse 84: "And you, at that time, [are] looking on."

﴿وأنْتُمْ﴾ means: "and the state is that you," i.e., you who are sitting around the dying person, grieving for him, ﴿حِينَئِذٍ﴾ — "at that time," meaning at the time when the soul has reached that place (the throat).

Since their sight, because it does not penetrate the inner (hidden) reality, is like nothing, [Allah] said: ﴿تَنْظُرُونَ﴾ — "you look on." That is, you have the attribute of staring at him, but you have no means and can do nothing except look. He did not say "تُبْصِرُونَ" (you perceive), lest it be thought that they have perception by sight of any of the hidden things, including the reality of the soul or anything else close to it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 85:

﴿Nahnu﴾ (We are), that is, while the reality is that We, with the majesty that is Ours, are ﴿nearer to him﴾, that is, to the dying person, in reality, by Our knowledge and Our complete power and Our angels, ﴿than you are﴾, despite the intensity of your nearness to him, ﴿but you do not see﴾, that is, even with your gazing at him, there is no effect from that gazing beyond its utmost (which is seeing) due to Our nearness to him, nor (do you see) Our angels who are entrusted with seizing his soul, so that you may know that the act belongs to Us and not to other than Us. Thus nothing of this attribute renews for you, so that you may grasp through it the reality of what he is in. Thus what We have informed about is established: the exclusivity with the inner knowledge and power, which We have expressed by the nearness that is the strongest of its causes.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 86:

Since the discourse was for establishing these important matters before the answer of "law-la" (lawla, "if not/were it not"), he repeated them for emphasis and clarification, and said: ﴿Then why, if you are not subject to judgment?﴾ O you who deny (p-243) the Resurrection and other matters, ﴿not subject to judgment﴾, meaning: subdued, owned, unrequited, and called to account for what you did in the abode of trial in which the Most Wise of judges placed you, since you refrain from being repaid by yourselves, or from others preventing you from it. The root of the form (dana, "to be indebted/subject") is for submission and subjugation, as stated by al-Baydawi.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 87:

﴿Why do you not return it﴾, i.e., the soul, to what it was, ﴿if you are truthful﴾, i.e., in a settled state, ﴿truthful﴾ in your claim that you are not compelled to refuse the summons of the mighty King who placed you in this abode for trial and testing, and that your affairs are not in the hands of anyone other than Him; and in your denial of what He reports to you of worldly matters, you expend your gratitude. This is evidence that there is no life at all for one whose soul has reached the throat. This is an argument against them for the resurrection, whose essence is this: if He, glory be to Him, does not restore you, then it is not He who decreed death upon you; and if [He] did not decree it, then why do you not avert it from yourselves, since it is among the grave calamities whose cure cannot be attained, while you treat its preliminaries. If you say: it is decreed and its cure is impossible, it necessarily follows that you affirm that resurrection is decreed and its cure is impossible. So if you deny one of the two, then deny the other, and if you affirm one of the two, then affirm the other; otherwise there is nothing but obstinacy. If you say: [we] do not know that He decreed it, then know that, had it not been by His decree, its repelling would have been possible at some time, especially since souls are disposed to dislike it, and among the dead are the wise and the kings. Its clarification is that you have exceeded in denying the signs of God, exalted is He, and His acts in every matter: if He sends a messenger to you, you say: "A lying sorcerer"; and if his Sender confirms him with a miraculous Book, you say: "Sorcery, fabrication, and a strange matter"; and if He provides you with rain from the water by which every thing lives, which revives you (p-244) by it, you say: "The star of such-and-such has brought it," in a state that leads to idleness, neglect and futility. Then why do you not return the soul to the body when it reaches the throat, if there is no governor of this existence through sending and sending down, the outpouring and seizing of souls, and the raising of servants for their requital for what they did in that wherein He placed them? This is an illustration with the acts of kings as is customary. Just as the kings of this world send none of their subjects to anyone to seize him by force except for requital, how then can it be supposed of the King of kings otherwise? Then the kings of this world would be wiser than Him. If He is not in full power, then do to His messengers as you do to the messengers of kings, for the one sought is often freed from them by some kind of deliverance after reaching the door of [the King]. His sending, glory be to Him, is like the sending of kings, except that, owing to the completeness of His power, He seizes with a seizing that no one can repel, and no one follows his seized one at all, neither to serve him after the seizing nor to lighten for him anything of what he is in, by other than what He, glory be to Him, has commanded through the tongues of His messengers of supplication and charity, nor to know his state in any manner [of the ways]. Rather, the matter is as it has been said:

*When a man is absent, his talk is concealed,* ∗∗∗ *and thoughts do not report of him anything that suffices.*

Since the implied meaning is that no one at all can return the soul once it has reached that place, because We intend to gather all creatures for judgment on account of what they did in what We placed them in and commanded them to do, and nothing happens except what We intend, then just as you acknowledge that He created you from dust and that He will compel you to return to dust, it necessarily follows that you must acknowledge that He is capable of returning you from the dust. [It necessarily follows that you must acknowledge that He is able to return you (p. 245) from the dust.] If you deny this necessary consequence, you must deny what it entails, and that is obstinate denial of what is plainly perceived. So let the other point be likewise. Thus it is established that We only return creatures to the dust in order to gather them there, then raise them from it, so that We may recompense each according to what he deserves, and divide them into three pairs. ﴿Then if he is﴾ — that is, the dead person — ﴿among those brought near﴾, that is, the foremost, whom the Truth drew to Himself from their own selves, so He brought them near to Him, and they were willed (muradun) before they became willing (muridun). Nearness here is not nearness of place, since He, may He be exalted, is far above that. It is rather by adopting the noble attributes (al-takhalluq bi'l-sifat, i.e., moral conformity to the divine qualities) to the extent of human capacity, so that the human being becomes pure spirit, like the angels, with no path for personal portions (ḥuẓūẓ) or desires (shahawat) to reach him. Their nearness is only by stripping off will entirely and at its root, because they have no desires, and so no aims, and so no action except what they were commanded. Thus there is no will, for will belongs only to the Master, glorified is He, and this is the meaning of ﴿He forbids immorality, wrongdoing and oppression﴾ [al-Nahl: 90], that is, absolute will apart from a command from God, because the owned slave, who belongs to another, should not have anything of his own, neither will nor anything else. May God, exalted is He, grant us success in that.

Then for him is rest and provision, and a mercy: that which refreshes him of the breeze of the wind. The meaning of Ya'qub's reading with a ḍamma (fa-rawḥ, pronounced with the ḍamma) is tranquility in the heart, calm, and a life after which there is no death. ﴿And sweet basil﴾, that is, abundant provision and a good, bright plant, and blossoms of fragrant scent.

When he mentioned this delight, he mentioned what gathers it and other than it, saying: ﴿And gardens﴾, that is, an orchard comprising fruits and sweet herbs, and what comes from them and from which they come. (p-246) Since the gardens of this world may contain some distress, he attached this garden to what is meant by these gardens, to inform that it is never free of it, saying: ﴿of bliss﴾, that is, there is nothing in them other than it; rather, they are restricted to it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 56, verse 90:

﴿And as for if he was﴾, that is, the deceased one among them, ﴿of the companions of the right﴾, that is, those who are the second rank among the companions of the right hand (al-maymanah).

﴿فَسَلامٌ﴾ [أيْ سَلامَةٌ] ونَجاةٌ وأمْرٌ وقَوْلٌ دالٌّ عَلَيْهِ. ولَمّا كانَ ما يُواجَهُ بِهِ الشَّرِيفُ مِن ذَلِكَ أعْلى قالَ: ﴿لَكَ﴾ أيْ: يا أعْلى الخَلْقِ أوْ يا أيُّها المُخاطَبُ.

ولَمّا كانَ مَن [أصابَ] السَّلامَ عَلى وجْهٍ مِنَ الوُجُوهِ فائِزًا، فَكَيْفَ إذا كانَ مَصْدَرًا لِلسَّلامِ ومَنبَعًا مِنهُ قالَ: ﴿مِن أصْحابِ اليَمِينِ﴾ أيْ أنَّهم في غايَةٍ [مِنَ] السَّلامَةِ وإظْهارِ السَّلامِ، لا يُدْرَكُ وصْفُها، وهو تَمْيِيزٌ (tamyiz: an accusative noun of specification) فِيهِ مَعْنى التَّعْجِيبِ، فَإنَّ إضافَتَهُ لَمْ تُفِدْهُ تَعْرِيفًا، وفي اللّامِ ”ومِن“ مُبالَغَةٌ في ذَلِكَ، فالمَعْنى: فَأمّا هم فَعَجَبًا لَكَ وأنْتَ أعْلى النّاسِ في كُلِّ مَعْنًى، وأعْرَفُهم بِكُلِّ أمْرٍ غَرِيبٍ مِنهم في سَلامَتِهِمْ وسَلامِهِمْ وتَعافِيهِمْ ومُلْكِهِمْ وشَرَفِهِمْ وعُلُوِّ مَقامِهِمْ، وذَلِكَ كُلُّهُ إنَّما أعْطَوْهُ لِأجْلِكَ زِيادَةً في شَرَفِكَ لِاتِّباعِهِمْ لِدِينِكَ، فَهو مِثْلُ قَوْلِ القائِلِ حَيْثُ قالَ:

؎فَيا لَكَ مِن لَيْلٍ كَأنَّ نُجُومَهُ ∗∗∗ بِكُلِّ مُغارِ الفَتْلِ شُدَّتْ بِيَذْبُلِ

*O what a night it is, its stars as though every tightly twisted rope had bound them to Yadhbul.*

وقَوْلِ القائِلِ أيْضًا حَيْثُ قالَ:

؎لِلَّهِ دَرُّ أنُو شِرْوانَ مِن رَجُلٍ ∗∗∗ ما كانَ أعْرَفَهُ بِالدُّونِ والسُّفْلِ

*By God, what a man Anushirvan was! How well he knew the lowly and the base.*

أيْ عَجَبًا لَكَ مِن لَيْلٍ وعَجَبًا مِن أنُو شِرْوانَ.

(p-247) When He had mentioned the two saved categories, He followed them with the lost, gathering them together under a single category, because the one for whom happiness is willed is sufficed by that, while the one who is sealed with wretchedness is not benefited by that harshness and abundance of words. So He said: ﴿And as for if he was﴾, i.e., that one whom We have taken from the companions of the left hand, while you are around him, your livers cut off for him, and you have no power over him at all, ﴿of the deniers﴾.

Since the denier is sometimes an obstinate opponent and sometimes an ignorant one who limits himself to what he has, He said: ﴿the astray﴾, i.e., the companions of the left, who were directed toward the way of guidance but turned away from it because of their negligence regarding the Resurrection.

﴿Then a welcome﴾, meaning for them. A welcome is what is prepared for the one who arrives, in keeping with what has been made apparent, ﴿of boiling water﴾, meaning water that has reached its utmost [heat], after they have suffered from thirst, just as the companions of the right hand approach the basin, and just as the arriving guest hastens to it so that he may cool his burning thirst with it and wash his face and hands with it.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And burning in the Blazing Fire﴾ (wa-taṣliyatu jaḥīm).

The commentary (al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar): ﴿And burning in the Blazing Fire﴾, meaning: for them, after the hospitality (nuzul), they will be made to burn (yuṣlawā) in the fire that is intensely blazing, a great burning.

When the proof of the resurrection had been completed in this sound and clear manner, and they were still denying it despite the clarity, he turned the address away from them to the most perfect of creation, and emphasized it so that they would hear. He said, driving it in the manner of a conclusion: ﴿Indeed, this﴾, i.e., what was mentioned in this surah concerning the resurrection, which they denied in their saying: ﴿"When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 47], and concerning the establishment of the proofs for it. Since it is manifest to a degree that nothing else equals it in this respect, he increased the emphasis in the form of restriction, saying: (p-248) ﴿it is indeed the truth of certainty﴾, i.e., because of what it rests upon of decisive, observable proofs, it is as if it were directly witnessed. Al-Asbahani said: Qatadah said concerning this verse: Indeed Allah, mighty and majestic, does not leave anyone among the people without bringing him to certainty through this Qur'an. As for the believer, he attains certainty in this world, and it benefits him; as for the hypocrite, he attains certainty on the Day of Resurrection, when it does not benefit him. End.
